title: China crude demand return on high fuel exports, what's next?
section_path: China crude demand return on high fuel exports, what's next?
section_path_text: China crude demand return on high fuel exports, what's next?
summary:
Main
China sees crude imports top 10mbd towards year-end, though momentum may fade once fuel exports normalise; stockpile will emerge as the next demand engine. By Emma Li
China's seaborne crude imports are set to recover to pre-war levels, supported by higher year-end fuel export quotas and stronger refinery runs aimed at utilising those allocations. November crude arrivals are expected to surge 25% month-on-month to 10.4mbd, broadly matching the 2025 average, while December volumes are likely to remain above the 10mbd mark.

children.title: A subtle rebalancing between BRICS and OPEC
section_path: A subtle rebalancing between BRICS and OPEC
children.section_path_text: A subtle rebalancing between BRICS and OPEC
children.summary: While China anticipates strong crude arrivals from the Middle East Gulf in Q4 [link to insight], the country experienced over 3.5mbd in supply losses during the war (covering China-bound crude exports from March 1 to November 20), including nearly 1mbd from Iran and 2mbd from other Middle Eastern producers. Conversely, supplies from fellow BRICS members Russia and Brazil have held remarkably firm, despite Russian barrels coming under full sanctions late last year.

children.title: The next demand engine: structural stock expansion over mere replenishment
section_path: The next demand engine: structural stock expansion over mere replenishment
children.section_path_text: The next demand engine: structural stock expansion over mere replenishment
children.summary: Onshore crude stock drawdowns in China have slowed significantly from September's record pace as seaborne cargo arrivals pick up. Overall, China drew down nearly 150mb of crude held in aboveground tanks during the Hormuz crisis.
